name: Dzongri and Goecha La
tagline: Sikkim's classic high trek, from Yuksom to the face of Kangchenjunga
meta_description: Dzongri and the Goecha La trek from Yuksom: route, camps, permits, best months, Dzongri Top sunrise, Samiti Lake and honest 2026 trek costs.
summary: Dzongri, at about 4,020 m, is the high meadow camp on the Yuksom–Goecha La trek inside Khangchendzonga National Park. The round trip takes about 8–10 days on foot, roughly 90 km, with a registered agency and licensed guide. Go April–May or October–November. Group treks cost about ₹14,000–25,000 per person, indicative, 2026.
intro: The Goecha La trek is the best-known high walk in Sikkim. It starts and ends at Yuksom, 1,780 m, and climbs through forest to Sachen and Tshoka, then up to the open slopes of Dzongri at about 4,020 m. From there the trail drops to the Prek Chu valley, runs up to Thansing and Lamuney, passes Samiti Lake and ends below the south-east face of Kangchenjunga. Goecha La itself is listed at 4,940 m on Wikipedia, and the round trip is about 90 km of walking.

Dzongri is the turning point of the trek. Most groups spend a rest day here to acclimatise, and use it to climb Dzongri Top before dawn. From the ridge you see a long line of peaks, among them Kangchenjunga, Kabru, Rathong, Kokthang and Pandim, at 6,691 m. On a clear October morning this view alone justifies the effort. The camp is cold, often windy and well above the tree line, so nights can drop below freezing even in spring and autumn.

This is a serious trek, not a stroll. You need a registered agency, a licensed guide and a park permit from the forest checkpost at Yuksom, and foreign nationals need a separate trek permit arranged through the agency. Many groups now turn back at Viewpoint 1, at about 4,600 m, and whether trekkers may go further depends on current forest department rules. We plan this trek in detail with our partners, and we always say: check current status before you travel.

story.title: The summit two climbers chose not to tread
paras: Kangchenjunga, at 8,586 m, is the third-highest mountain in the world. For the Lepcha people it is Kongchen Kongchlo, and in Lepcha tradition the first Lepcha couple were made from the snows of its summit. For Sikkim as a whole it is a guardian deity, honoured each year at Pang Lhabsol. That reverence shaped one of the most unusual moments in mountaineering, and you are walking towards the mountain it concerns when you climb above Dzongri.

In 1955 a British expedition led by Charles Evans attempted the mountain from the Nepal side. Before they set out, they promised Sikkim's ruler, Chogyal Tashi Namgyal, that the very top would stay untrodden. On 25 May 1955 Joe Brown and George Band climbed to within a few feet of the summit and stopped there, keeping the promise. Norman Hardie and Tony Streather reached the same point the next day and also stopped short.

Many climbers since then have kept the same custom, stopping just below the true top. On the Indian side the mountain remains closed to climbing expeditions, out of respect for its place in Sikkimese belief. From Dzongri Top and from the viewpoints near Goecha La you see the south-east face of that untrodden summit. It is worth knowing the story before you get there; it changes how you look at the mountain at dawn.
story.source: Wikipedia: 'Kangchenjunga', '1955 British Kangchenjunga expedition', 'Joe Brown (climber)', 'George Band', 'Goecha La'; the Lepcha origin story is oral tradition

did_you_know: Khangchendzonga National Park, through which the whole Goecha La trail runs, became India's first 'mixed' UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.
Samiti Lake on the Goecha La trail lies at about 4,200 m and is considered sacred by local people as a source of the Prek Chu river.
Mount Pandim, which towers over the upper Goecha La valley, is 6,691 m high.

highlights.title: Sunrise from Dzongri Top
highlights.text: On the acclimatisation day at Dzongri, groups climb the ridge above camp in the dark and wait for first light. Kangchenjunga, Kabru, Rathong, Kokthang and Pandim catch the sun one after another. It is bitterly cold before dawn, so take a down jacket, gloves and a hot drink.

highlights.title: Rhododendron forests below Tshoka
highlights.text: Between Sachen, Tshoka and Phedang the trail climbs through forests of oak, magnolia and many kinds of rhododendron. In April and early May they flower in reds, pinks and whites. Listen for blood pheasants, Sikkim's state bird, scratching on the forest floor.

highlights.title: Samiti Lake
highlights.text: Above Lamuney, at about 4,200 m, Samiti Lake lies in the Onglakthang valley below Pandim. Local people consider it sacred as a source of the Prek Chu. Walk around it quietly, do not wash or throw anything in the water, and look for the mountain's reflection on still mornings.

highlights.title: Viewpoint 1 and Goecha La
highlights.text: The final push leaves Lamuney or Thansing at about 2–3 am for Viewpoint 1, at about 4,600 m, facing Kangchenjunga's south-east face. Goecha La itself is 4,940 m. How far groups may go changes with forest department rules, so check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: A rest day that matters
highlights.text: The extra night at Dzongri is not a luxury. Going from 1,780 m at Yuksom to about 4,020 m in three days is a big gain, and the rest day helps your body adjust. Walk a little higher during the day, drink plenty of water and sleep lower.

how_to_reach.text: First reach Yuksom, the trailhead. Take a shared jeep from Siliguri to Gyalshing (₹400–550 a seat) or from Gangtok to Gyalshing (₹350–500), then on to Yuksom (₹120–180). Departures to Yuksom are few, so most trekkers arrive in Pelling or Gyalshing the day before. Fares are indicative, 2026; check current status before you travel.

Many agencies arrange a shared or reserved vehicle from NJP or Bagdogra to Yuksom as part of the package, a long day of 6.5–8 hours. If you hire your own, a car from NJP or Bagdogra to Pelling costs about ₹5,500–7,500 and Pelling to Yuksom about ₹2,000–2,800, indicative, 2026.

The nearest railhead is New Jalpaiguri (NJP), and the nearest reliable airport is Bagdogra (IXB). Plan to arrive in Siliguri by midday the day before your drive, or a full day before the trek starts. Keep a buffer day at the end too, as rain or road closures can delay the return.

From Yuksom the trail runs about 10 km to Sachen, 7 km to Tshoka and 10 km to Dzongri. From Dzongri it is about 10 km to Thansing, then on to Lamuney, Samiti Lake and the viewpoints, before returning by Thansing and Tshoka to Yuksom. Total walking is about 90 km over 8–10 days.

where_to_stay: Before and after the trek you stay in Yuksom, where Hotel Yangrigang on the main road is a long-standing budget base for trekkers and family homestays cost about ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day with meals, indicative, 2026. On the trail there are no hotels. Agencies use the forest department trekkers' huts at Sachen, Tshoka, Dzongri, Thansing and Lamuney where available, and pitch tents at the same camps. Huts are basic: wooden bunks, no heating and shared toilets. Bring or rent a warm sleeping bag rated well below freezing, even in May.

budget_tip: Join a fixed-departure group trek from Yuksom rather than a private one; you share the guide, cook and pack animals, and the price drops from ₹35,000 or more to about ₹14,000–25,000 per person, indicative, 2026.
tips: Do not skip the rest day at Dzongri; it is the single best thing you can do to avoid altitude sickness.
Break in your boots before you come and carry two pairs of thick socks for every three days.
Pack everything in plastic bags inside your rucksack, as sudden rain and snow are common even in October.
Carry all your rubbish back to Yuksom; plastic is a big problem in the park and rangers may check.
Rules on group size, campsites and how far you may go change from season to season; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Sunrise from Dzongri Top
experiences.best_time: Rest day at Dzongri, Oct–Nov and Apr–May
experiences.summary: On the acclimatisation day, groups climb the ridge above Dzongri camp in darkness and watch the sun light up a long wall of peaks, from Kabru and Kangchenjunga to Pandim. It is the most famous view on the trek, and on a clear morning it is worth every cold minute.
body: Your guide will wake you at about 3:30 or 4 am. The climb to Dzongri Top from camp is short, usually 45 minutes to an hour, but you are already at around 4,000 m, so you will feel every step. Walk slowly, breathe through your nose if you can, and stop often. Wear everything warm you have: thermals, fleece, down jacket, hat, gloves and a buff. A head torch is essential.

On the top, prayer flags snap in the wind and the sky slowly turns grey and then orange. The first peaks to catch the light are the highest. Kangchenjunga, at 8,586 m, glows first, then Kabru, Rathong and Kokthang, and Pandim, at 6,691 m, closer and darker to the right. On a really clear day the view runs along a long arc of the eastern Himalaya, and your guide will name each peak.

Stay for about an hour after sunrise, then walk back down for breakfast. Most groups spend the rest of the day around camp, resting, drinking water and perhaps walking a little higher in the afternoon to help their bodies adjust. Clouds often build by mid-morning, so the dawn view is the one to aim for. If the morning is cloudy, ask your guide whether there is time to try again the next day.

faqs.q: How high is Dzongri Top
faqs.a: Dzongri camp sits at about 4,020 m, and Dzongri Top, the ridge above it, is a little higher. The climb from camp usually takes 45 minutes to an hour. Because you are already high, walk slowly and stop if you feel dizzy or breathless. Tell your guide at once if you have a headache that will not go.

faqs.q: Which peaks can you see from Dzongri Top
faqs.a: On a clear morning you see Kangchenjunga (8,586 m) with Kabru, Rathong, Kokthang, Frey Peak and Pandim (6,691 m), among others. Wikipedia notes that about twelve Himalayan summits are visible from Dzongri Top, Thansing and Goecha La. Your guide will help you name them, as the peaks look different from every angle.

faqs.q: What is the best month for the Dzongri sunrise
faqs.a: October and early November give the clearest skies and the best chance of a cloudless sunrise, though nights are very cold. April and May also work and add flowering rhododendrons lower down, but haze and afternoon cloud are more common. From June to August the trek does not normally run because of the monsoon.

experiences.title: Samiti Lake below Pandim
experiences.summary: Samiti Lake lies at about 4,200 m in the Onglakthang valley, below Mount Pandim and the Kangchenjunga massif. Local people consider it sacred as a source of the Prek Chu. Most trekkers pass it in the dark on summit morning, so a daylight visit is a quiet reward.
body: Samiti Lake sits above Lamuney, the last camp before Goecha La, in a wide glacial valley called Onglakthang. Wikipedia gives its height as about 4,200–4,300 m and its width as up to 230 m when it is full. The water is clear and green, and on still mornings the peaks around it reflect on the surface. It freezes in winter and thaws in spring, when small plants and flowers appear around its edges.

Most groups walk past the lake in the dark at about 3 am on the way to Viewpoint 1 and see it properly only on the way back. If your group camps at Lamuney, ask your guide whether you can walk up in the afternoon before summit day. It is an easy walk of under an hour from Lamuney, and it is a good way to test how you feel at this height before the big early start.

The lake is known locally in Sikkimese as Bunmoten Choo and is considered sacred as a source of the Prek Chu, the river that runs past Thansing. Treat it with respect. Do not wash, throw stones or leave anything in the water, and keep your voice down. Sit on the moraine for a while and look up at Pandim, which rises steeply above the lake to 6,691 m. Then walk back slowly; you will need the energy later.

faqs.q: How high is Samiti Lake
faqs.a: Samiti Lake sits at about 4,200–4,300 m in the Onglakthang valley on the Goecha La trail, above the camp at Lamuney. It is one of the highest points most trekkers reach before Viewpoint 1. Take it slowly at this height, drink plenty of water, and tell your guide about any headache or nausea.

faqs.q: Can you camp at Samiti Lake
faqs.a: Camping rules on the Goecha La trail are set by the forest department and change from season to season. In recent years most groups have camped at Thansing or Lamuney and walked past Samiti Lake on summit morning. Your agency will know the current rule; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Samiti Lake frozen in winter
faqs.a: Yes. Samiti Lake freezes in winter and thaws in spring. By late October nights are well below freezing and the edges may ice over, and from December to February the area is usually under snow, when the trek is not normally run. April and May bring melting snow and new growth around the lake.

experiences.title: Summit morning to Viewpoint 1
experiences.duration: 8–10 hours return from Thansing or Lamuney
experiences.summary: The hardest and highest day of the trek: a 2–3 am start, a slow climb in the dark past Samiti Lake and up the moraine to Viewpoint 1 at about 4,600 m, facing the south-east face of Kangchenjunga at sunrise. Whether you may go further towards Goecha La depends on current rules.
body: Summit day starts at about 2 or 3 am from Lamuney or Thansing. You walk by head torch past Samiti Lake and along the moraine of the Onglakthang glacier, climbing steadily to Viewpoint 1, at about 4,600 m. It takes most groups three to four hours to get there. The air is thin and very cold, so walk slowly, eat a little every hour and keep a water bottle inside your jacket so it does not freeze.

At sunrise the wall in front of you lights up. This is the south-east face of Kangchenjunga, the side that Sikkim looks at, with the summit that the 1955 climbers chose not to tread. Pandim rises to your right. Goecha La itself is listed at 4,940 m and lies further up the valley. In recent seasons many groups have been allowed only as far as Viewpoint 1, so ask your agency and check current status before you travel.

Turn back by mid-morning, before the wind and cloud build. The descent to Thansing takes several hours, and most people feel tired but very happy. Do not push on if anyone in your group shows signs of altitude sickness such as a bad headache, confusion or vomiting; the only cure is going down. A good guide will make that call for you, and you should accept it without argument. The mountain will still be there next season.

faqs.q: Can trekkers go up to Goecha La pass
faqs.a: It depends on the current rules. In recent seasons many groups have been allowed only as far as Viewpoint 1, at about 4,600 m, and not all the way to Goecha La at 4,940 m. The forest department sets these limits and changes them from year to year. Ask your agency and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Goecha La trek
faqs.a: It is a moderate to difficult high-altitude trek of about 90 km over 8–10 days, reaching about 4,600 m or higher. You need good fitness, comfort walking 6–8 hours a day and the patience to acclimatise. Beginners who train for two or three months and go with a good agency usually manage it well.

faqs.q: What time do you start for Goecha La viewpoint
faqs.a: Groups usually leave Lamuney or Thansing between 2 and 3 am to reach Viewpoint 1 by sunrise, when the sky is clearest and the light falls on Kangchenjunga's south-east face. The climb takes about three to four hours. Carry a head torch with spare batteries, warm gloves and water kept inside your jacket.

experiences.title: Rhododendron forests between Sachen and Tshoka
experiences.summary: The lower part of the trek, from Yuksom through Sachen to Tshoka and on to Phedang, climbs through thick forest of oak, magnolia and rhododendron. In April and early May the trees flower in reds, pinks and whites, and the forest is full of birds. It is the gentlest part of the trek.
body: The first two days of the trek run through Khangchendzonga National Park's lower forests. From Yuksom, at 1,780 m, the trail crosses side streams on suspension bridges and climbs to Sachen, at about 2,200 m, then to Tshoka, at about 3,000 m. The forest is dense and damp, with moss, ferns and orchids on the trunks. In spring it smells of wet earth and flowers, and in autumn it is cool and quiet.

Above Tshoka the trail turns to wooden planks and stone steps through rhododendron forest towards Phedang. In April and early May the trees flower in waves of red, pink and white. The tree rhododendron, Rhododendron arboreum, is one of many species here. Bloom times change with height and with each year's weather, so the lower trees can be finished while the higher ones are just beginning. Ask your agency for recent reports before you book.

This is also the best section for birds. Look and listen for blood pheasants, Sikkim's state bird, and with luck a Himalayan monal or satyr tragopan in the higher forest. Walk slowly, keep your voice down and stop often. There is no hurry: most groups reach Tshoka by early afternoon. If you see a red panda, count yourself very lucky; they live in these forests but are rarely seen. Never feed any animal or bird on the trail.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom on the Goecha La trek
faqs.a: Rhododendrons on the Goecha La trail usually flower from about late March to early May, with the best show around April between Tshoka and Phedang. Lower trees bloom first and higher ones later. Bloom times change each year with weather and snow, so ask your agency for recent reports before you book.

faqs.q: Can I do a short trek to Tshoka only
faqs.a: Some agencies offer shorter treks from Yuksom to Tshoka or Dzongri and back, which take in the forests and the Dzongri Top view without going to Goecha La. You still need a registered agency, a guide and a park permit from the Yuksom checkpost. Ask about current options and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What wildlife can I see on the Goecha La trek
faqs.a: In the forests you may see blood pheasants, Sikkim's state bird, plus laughingthrushes, and with luck a Himalayan monal or satyr tragopan. Higher up, yaks and dzos carry loads for some groups. Red pandas and other mammals live in the park but are rarely seen. Walk quietly in the early morning for the best chances.

faqs.q: How many days is the Goecha La trek
faqs.a: Most itineraries take 8–10 days of walking from Yuksom and back, or 9–11 nights including travel from Siliguri. A typical plan is Yuksom, Sachen, Tshoka, Dzongri with a rest day, Thansing, Lamuney, Viewpoint 1, then back by Thansing and Tshoka to Yuksom. Total walking is about 90 km.

faqs.q: How much does the Goecha La trek cost
faqs.a: A group trek with a registered agency costs about ₹14,000–25,000 per person, indicative, 2026, usually covering food, tents or huts, guide, cook, pack animals or porters and permits. A private trek costs ₹35,000 or more per person. Add travel to and from Yuksom and a night there at each end.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for the Goecha La trek
faqs.a: Yes. The trek runs inside Khangchendzonga National Park, so you need a park permit from the forest checkpost at Yuksom and must go with a registered agency and a licensed guide. Foreign nationals also need a trek permit arranged through the agency, normally for groups of two or more. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Goecha La trek safe for beginners
faqs.a: It is possible for fit beginners who train for two or three months, go with a good agency and respect the acclimatisation day at Dzongri. The main risk is altitude sickness above 4,000 m. If you have heart or lung conditions, talk to your doctor first. Never hide symptoms from your guide.

faqs.q: What is the best time for the Goecha La trek
faqs.a: October and early November are best for clear mountain views, with cold nights. April and May are second best, with rhododendrons in bloom but more haze and cloud. March and December are possible but cold and snowy. The trek is not normally run from June to August, and January and February are closed by snow in practice.

faqs.q: How high is Dzongri
faqs.a: Dzongri camp is at about 4,020 m, reached on the third day from Yuksom by way of Sachen and Tshoka. It is the first high camp on the Goecha La trek, above the tree line, and most groups spend two nights there to acclimatise. Expect freezing nights and strong wind, even in spring and autumn.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network on the Goecha La trek
faqs.a: Mobile network is weak or absent above Yuksom, with occasional signal at a few points depending on your operator. Plan to be offline for most of the trek. Tell family your dates in advance, and carry a power bank because there is no charging on the trail. Your agency may carry a radio or satellite phone for emergencies.

faqs.q: Can I do the Goecha La trek without a guide
faqs.a: No. Rules for Khangchendzonga National Park require trekkers to go with a registered agency and a licensed guide, and the park permit is issued on that basis at the Yuksom checkpost. Solo or unguided trekking is not allowed. These rules are enforced and can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Dzongri trek different from Goecha La trek
faqs.a: Dzongri is a camp and viewpoint on the way to Goecha La. A Dzongri trek usually means a shorter loop from Yuksom to Dzongri and back, about 5–6 days, for the Dzongri Top sunrise. The full Goecha La trek continues to Thansing, Lamuney, Samiti Lake and Viewpoint 1, taking 8–10 days.
